claims.text: The feedstock is AlCrFeNiSi powder with a typical particle-size distribution and as-received purity.
Controlled ultrasonic vibration is introduced into the melt pool during additive manufacturing.
Enhanced melt-pool dynamics promote more uniform nucleation.
Enhanced melt-pool dynamics produce uniform grain refinement throughout the component.
Ultrasonic vibration induces acoustic streaming in the AlCrFeNiSi melt pool.
Ultrasonic vibration induces cavitation in the AlCrFeNiSi melt pool.
Acoustic streaming and cavitation disrupt thermal hotspots.
Acoustic streaming and cavitation homogenize cooling.
Disruption of thermal hotspots and homogenization of cooling reduce thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal gradients and refined microstructure mitigate residual stress.
Ultrasonically processed components will have statistically significantly lower residual thermal stresses than components made without ultrasonic vibration.
Ultrasonically processed components will have finer and more uniformly distributed grains than components made without ultrasonic vibration.
Ultrasonically processed components will exhibit increased tensile strength relative to components made without ultrasonic vibration.
Ultrasonically processed components will exhibit increased ductility relative to components made without ultrasonic vibration.
The hypothesis applies to miniature components produced in controlled high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing environments.
The optimal ultrasonic frequency and amplitude depend on systematic optimization and possible interactions with additive-manufacturing parameters.
